prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f(x)=ax+b$ with $a\ne0$ and $b$ real numbers. Find all pairs of real constants $c$ and $d$ with $c\ne0$ such that $g(x)=cx+d$ commutes with $f(x)$.
answer:
$d(a-1)=b(c-1)$. For $a
e1$: $d=\dfrac{b(c-1)}{a-1}$ with any $c
e0$. For $a=1,b=0$: all $c
e0$, all $d$. For $a=1,b
e0$: $c=1$ and all $d$.

solutions.title: Compare the compositions
solutions.body:
$f(g(x))=a(cx+d)+b=acx+ad+b$ and $g(f(x))=c(ax+b)+d=acx+bc+d$. These agree for all $x$ iff $ad+b=bc+d$, i.e.
$$d(a-1)=b(c-1).$$
* If $a
e1$: $d=\dfrac{b(c-1)}{a-1}$, with $c
e0$ arbitrary.
* If $a=1$ the condition is $b(c-1)=0$: when $b=0$ every $c
e0$ and every $d$ works; when $b
e0$ we need $c=1$, with $d$ arbitrary.

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f(x)=ax^b$ with $a\ne0$ real and $b$ a positive integer. Find all pairs of real numbers $d$ and $c$ with $c\ne0$ such that $g(x)=cx^d$ commutes with $f(x)$.

solutions.title: Compare the compositions
solutions.body:
For $x>0$ (so that real powers make sense; for a nonnegative integer $d$ the computation holds for all $x$):
$$g(f(x))=c\,(ax^b)^d=c\,a^dx^{bd},\qquad f(g(x))=a\,(cx^d)^b=a\,c^bx^{bd}.$$
The powers of $x$ agree, so the functions commute iff $c\,a^d=a\,c^b$; dividing by $ac\ne0$,
$$c^{\,b-1}=a^{\,d-1}.$$
Solving for $c$ when $b\ge2$: if $b-1$ is odd there is exactly one real $c$ (the real $(b-1)$-th root of $a^{d-1}$); if $b-1$ is even, there are two, $c=\pm(a^{d-1})^{1/(b-1)}$, when $a^{d-1}>0$ and none otherwise. For $b=1$ the condition is $a^{d-1}=1$ (any $c$). Examples: $d=1$ gives $c^{b-1}=1$ (so $c=1$, and also $c=-1$ if $b$ is odd); $d=b$ gives $c=a$ (and $c=-a$ if $b$ is odd).

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f(x)=ax+b$ with $a,b$ real, $a\ne0$. Show that if $f(x)$ commutes with a polynomial $g(x)$ of degree $n\ge2$, then $a=\pm1$.
answer: Comparing leading coefficients of $g(ax+b)=a\,g(x)+b$ gives $a^{n-1}=1$, so $a=\pm1$.

solutions.title: Leading coefficients
solutions.body: Let $g(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots$ with $a_n\ne0$, $n\ge2$. Then $g(f(x))=g(ax+b)$ has leading term $a_na^nx^n$, while $f(g(x))=a\,g(x)+b$ has leading term $a\,a_nx^n$. Equating, $a^n=a$, and since $a\ne0$, $a^{n-1}=1$. A real number with $a^{n-1}=1$, $n-1\ge1$, is $1$ or $-1$. So $a=\pm1$. ∎

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f(x)=x+b$ ($a=1$). Take $g(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ with $a_n\ne0$ and $n\ge2$. Show that if $f(x)$ commutes with $g(x)$, then $b=0$, so $f(x)=x$.
answer: $g(x+b)-g(x)=b$ forces $b=0$: otherwise the left side has degree $n-1\ge1$.

solutions.title: Compare degrees
solutions.body: Commuting means $g(x+b)=g(x)+b$, i.e. $g(x+b)-g(x)=b$ for all $x$. If $b\ne0$, the left side is a polynomial whose $x^{n-1}$ coefficient is $n\,a_n\,b\ne0$ (the $x^n$ terms cancel), so it has degree $n-1\ge1$, whereas the right side is the constant $b$. Contradiction. Hence $b=0$ and $f(x)=x$ (which of course commutes with every $g$). ∎

prompt: Let $f(x)=x+2\pi$. Find a non-polynomial function that commutes with $f(x)$.

solutions.title: Use periodicity
solutions.body: Take $g(x)=x+\sin x$. Then $g(f(x))=x+2\pi+\sin(x+2\pi)=x+2\pi+\sin x$ and $f(g(x))=x+\sin x+2\pi$. They are equal, and $g$ is not a polynomial. ∎

prompt: Let $f(x)=x+2\pi$. Show that there are infinitely many functions that commute with $f(x)$.
answer: $g_k(x)=x+k\sin x$ for every real $k$ (more generally $x+p(x)$ with $p$ $2\pi$-periodic).

solutions.title: A family
solutions.body: For each real $k$ let $g_k(x)=x+k\sin x$. Then $g_k(f(x))=x+2\pi+k\sin x=f(g_k(x))$, so every $g_k$ commutes with $f$, and different $k$ give different functions. More generally $g(x)=x+p(x)$ commutes with $f$ for any function $p$ of period $2\pi$. ∎

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $P(x)$ be an arbitrary fixed polynomial. Define $R_q^{(1)}(x)=xP(x^q)$ and $R_q^{(n+1)}(x)=R_q^{(1)}\bigl(R_q^{(n)}(x)\bigr)$ for $n\ge1$. For $q=2$ find constants $c_1\ne1$ and $c_2\ne1$ such that $c_1R_2^{(l)}(x)$ commutes with $c_2R_2^{(m)}(x)$ (for all positive integers $l,m$).

solutions.title: Oddness
solutions.body:
For $q=2$, $R_2^{(1)}(x)=xP(x^2)$ is an odd function, and a composition of odd functions is odd, so every $R_2^{(n)}$ is odd: $R_2^{(l)}(-y)=-R_2^{(l)}(y)$. Take $c_1=c_2=-1$. Then
$$(-R_2^{(l)})\bigl(-R_2^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=-R_2^{(l)}\bigl(-R_2^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=R_2^{(l)}\bigl(R_2^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=R_2^{(l+m)}(x),$$
and in the same way $(-R_2^{(m)})\circ(-R_2^{(l)})=R_2^{(m+l)}=R_2^{(l+m)}$. So they commute. ∎

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $P(x)$ be an arbitrary fixed polynomial and $q$ a positive integer. Define $R_q^{(1)}(x)=xP(x^q)$ and $R_q^{(n+1)}(x)=R_q^{(1)}\bigl(R_q^{(n)}(x)\bigr)$. Find constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that $c_1R_q^{(l)}(x)$ commutes with $c_2R_q^{(m)}(x)$.
answer: Any constants with $c_1^{\,q}=c_2^{\,q}=1$ work (real: $c_i=1$, and also $c_i=-1$ when $q$ is even).

solutions.title: Rotation symmetry
solutions.body:
If $c^q=1$ then $R_q^{(1)}(cx)=cx\,P(c^qx^q)=c\,R_q^{(1)}(x)$, and by induction $R_q^{(n)}(cx)=c\,R_q^{(n)}(x)$ for all $n$. Therefore, for $c_1^q=c_2^q=1$:
$$(c_1R_q^{(l)})\bigl(c_2R_q^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=c_1c_2\,R_q^{(l)}\bigl(R_q^{(m)}(x)\bigr)=c_1c_2R_q^{(l+m)}(x),$$
and the reverse order gives $c_2c_1R_q^{(m+l)}(x)$, the same. So all $c_1,c_2$ with $c_1^q=c_2^q=1$ work for every $P$. Over the reals these are $c_1,c_2\in\{1\}$ if $q$ is odd and $\{1,-1\}$ if $q$ is even (so for $q=2$, $c_1=c_2=-1$ is the nontrivial choice). ∎

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f_2(x)=x^2$. Find all polynomials $g(x)$ of degree greater than two that commute with $f_2(x)$.

solutions.title: Compare the top two terms
solutions.body: Commuting means $g(x^2)=g(x)^2$. Let $g(x)=a_nx^n+a_kx^k+\cdots$ where $a_kx^k$ is the next nonzero term, $k<n$ (if $g=a_nx^n$ alone there is nothing to compare). The leading coefficient gives $a_n=a_n^2$, so $a_n=1$. In $g(x)^2$ the coefficient of $x^{n+k}$ is $2a_k\ne0$ (only the product of the two top terms produces this exponent, since all other products have smaller exponent). In $g(x^2)$ every exponent is even and equals twice an exponent of $g$; the exponents of $g$ strictly between $k$ and $n$ do not exist, and $\frac{n+k}2$ lies strictly between $k$ and $n$, so $x^{n+k}$ does not appear in $g(x^2)$. Contradiction. Hence $g(x)=x^n$, and indeed $(x^2)^n=(x^n)^2$. ∎

prompt: Two functions $f$ and $g$ *commute* if $f(g(x))=g(f(x))$ for all $x$. Let $f_m(x)=x^m$ with $m\ge2$ an integer. Find all polynomials $g(x)$ of degree greater than two that commute with $f_m(x)$.

solutions.title: Compare the top two terms
solutions.body: Commuting means $g(x^m)=g(x)^m$. Let $g=a_nx^n+a_kx^k+\cdots$ with $a_kx^k$ the next nonzero term. Leading coefficients: $a_n=a_n^m$, so $a_n^{m-1}=1$: $a_n=1$, or $a_n=-1$ if $m$ is odd. In $g(x)^m$ the exponent $n(m-1)+k$ occurs only once (from $m-1$ copies of the top term and one copy of $a_kx^k$), with coefficient $m\,a_n^{m-1}a_k\ne0$. In $g(x^m)$ all exponents are multiples of $m$, namely $m\cdot(\text{exponent of }g)$, and $n(m-1)+k=m\cdot j$ with $j=n-\frac{n-k}m$ strictly between $k$ and $n$, an exponent $g$ does not have. Contradiction, so $g=a_nx^n$, and $g(x^m)=a_nx^{nm}$ equals $g(x)^m=a_n^mx^{nm}$ exactly when $a_n^{m-1}=1$. So $g=x^n$, or $g=-x^n$ for odd $m$. ∎
